10567-the-guardian-angel-ship-s-company-:
W. W. Jacobs published this comic tale as the seventh part of Ship's Company, told by the night-watchman. The watchman doubts philanthropists, saying kindness usually wants something in return, like a stranger who stood eight half-pints then borrowed five shillings. Sam Small's kindness to Ginger Dick and Peter Russet proves his point.

Sam, Ginger, and Peter, back from a voyage with money to spend, take a room in Wapping and fall out in a Poplar pub over a joke. A bet on drinking a pot of beer without breath starts the row, and a lodger going through pockets adds theft to comedy. Readers get a short, salty Jacobs tale of sailors, jokes, and false friends.
10787-the-toll-house-sailor-s-knots-part:
W. W. Jacobs's "The Toll-House," the seventh tale in Sailors' Knots from 1909, is his most famous ghost story. At the Three Feathers Inn, Jack Barnes scoffs at hauntings, calling noises wind in the chimney and rats in the wainscot. Meagle, pouring tea, admits a half belief in the supernatural and proposes a test in the toll-house itself.

The tale that follows plays fear against skepticism, as rational talk meets a house with a past. Jacobs builds dread slowly, through talk rather than shocks. Readers get a compact, chilling story, complete on its own, often ranked among the best short ghost tales in English.
11187-four-pigeons-captains-all-book-7:
Set at the Cauliflower inn in Claybury, this Jacobs story follows a talkative old man who cadges ale from strangers and repays them with a tale of shooting, poaching, and village cunning. Squire Rockett has let the Hall to a London gentleman, Sutton, whose shooting party draws the attention of Bob Pretty, Claybury's notorious poacher. Four pigeons become the center of a trick played on the visitors.

Jacobs keeps the comedy in the dialogue, letting the old man's wheedling and the poacher's cheek carry the plot. The story is slight, but its village world feels complete in a few pages. It shows why Jacobs's short fiction stayed popular: low stakes, sharp talk, and a twist that favors the local over the visitor.
11477-family-cares-deep-waters-part-7:
W.W. Jacobs's story opens with Mr. Jernshaw, weighing pound packets of sugar in his shop, surprised by Harry Barrett, a bronzed man of about forty who has come home after fifteen years. Barrett, who has done well enough in Melbourne, says he has come back for the evening of his life.

The trouble is family: children, uncles, and aunts, and a town that expects Barrett to take them in. Jernshaw presses the claim, Barrett resists it, and the story turns on what a returned man owes the kin he left behind. The humour stays dry, and the shop parlour stays the scene.
11889-clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of:
Volume 7 of Samuel Richardson's Clarissa Harlowe, in nine volumes, carries the heroine's story through letters between Clarissa and her friend Miss Howe. Howe begs Clarissa to take comfort and not despair, while fearing for her own safety from Mr. Lovelace, and offers an instruction to mothers drawn from the affair.

Clarissa, averse to appearing in court against Lovelace, nevertheless agrees to prosecute him rather than submit to his terms. Later letters show her glad to be released from confinement, naming Lovelace as the author of all her woes. The volume's power lies in its slow, letter-by-letter pressure, as Clarissa's moral reasoning meets Lovelace's persistence and her family's alarm.
12127-captain-rogers-the-lady-of-the-bar:
Part 7 of Jacobs's Lady of the Barge stories, Captain Rogers, opens with a man coming slowly over an old stone bridge. He averts his gaze from the dark river with its silent craft, looking with satisfaction toward the feeble lights of a small town. He walks with a painful, forced step, as one who has already trudged far, his worsted hose, where not darned, in holes.

Captain Rogers, like many of Jacobs's sailors ashore, is a man whose past has caught up with him. The story follows his return, recognition, and reckoning in a town that remembers him. Jacobs tells the tale in his plain, ironic manner, letting a tramp's worn stockings say as much as any confession.
12157-the-unknown-night-watches-part-7:
W. W. Jacobs wrote this short story for Night Watches, his 1911 collection of Thames-side comic tales. A night watchman narrates, and the joke grows from mistaken identity and a handsome man who cannot refuse a woman.

Captain Bill Smithers, a quiet schooner master, marries a widow who soon watches his every move, demands a daily log of his trips, and even sails with him. Worse, an old flame named Dorothy still writes, and Smithers begs the watchman to hide the letters. The tale follows his efforts to keep two lives apart as jealousy tightens around him. Jacobs keeps the tone light, but the comedy rests on a man trapped by his own good looks and weak refusals.
12207-establishing-relations-odd-craft-p:
Mr. Richard Catesby, second officer of the steamer Wizard, steps ashore in high good humor in Establishing Relations, a comic tale from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft. Wapping residents sit at open doors in the evening cool, ready to talk to anyone in earshot.

Catesby, turning into Bashford Lane, meets kin he never knew, or claims he never knew, and must establish relations on the spot. The comedy turns on sailor bluster meeting family expectation: who is related to whom, who owes what, and who will pay for supper. Jacobs keeps the dialect lively and the plot light. The story is a small farce of identity, where a night ashore becomes a family reunion no one quite planned.
13884-the-history-of-sir-charles-grandis:
Samuel Richardson's History of Sir Charles Grandison continues in this fourth volume, told in letters. Miss Harriet Byron writes to Miss Lucy Selby, reporting Dr. Bartlett's letters in turn. Sir Charles visits the whole Porretta family in Italy, whose characters show plainly on the occasion. His affectionate parting from Jeronymo closes the first letter.

Later letters follow Jeronymo's account of family talk after Sir Charles leaves. Lady G quarrels with her lord and seeks Miss Byron's help to reconcile. Kind advice restores good humour, though pride lingers. Richardson studies manners, virtue, and courtship at length. The volume shows epistolary fiction at its most detailed. Readers of Richardson will find his moral world intact.
16282-history-of-the-world-war-volume-3-:
Francis A. March's History of the World War, volume three, published by Leslie-Judge in New York in 1919, narrates the Great War with photographs by James H. Hare and Donald Thompson. Richard J. Beamish, special war correspondent and military analyst, collaborated, and General Peyton C. March, chief of staff of the United States Army, wrote the introduction. Official photographs from American, Canadian, British, French, and Italian governments illustrate the text.

Chapters cover Neuve Chapelle and war in blood-soaked trenches, Italy declaring war on Austria, and glorious Gallipoli, with attacks costing thousands of lives for every foot of ground. March writes an authentic narrative for general readers. The volume offers a contemporary, richly pictured account of 1915.
23405-journeys-through-bookland-vol-7:
Charles H. Sylvester compiled this seventh volume of Journeys Through Bookland, a new plan for reading the world's best literature for children, in a nineteen twenty two Chicago edition. Poems and tales follow a graded path, so a child meets fine writing in small, well chosen doses.

Wordsworth's daffodils, Burns on a mouse and a mountain daisy, Scott's boat song, and Irving's tale of a governor and a notary all appear. Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner also appears, with a canoe race and a petrified fern tale beside them. Notes and pictures guide the young reader, and each piece stands on its own while fitting the larger journey. Parents and teachers will value the set as a friendly door into classic verse and story.
27648-buchanan-s-journal-of-man-august-1:
Buchanan's Journal of Man, volume one, number seven, dated August 1887, mixes science, philosophy, and psychical inquiry. Its contents list Creation's Mysteries, a true poet, the poetry of peace and the practice of war, the Volapük language, and progress of the marvellous.

Miscellaneous intelligence covers photography perfected, the Cannon King, land monopoly, the grand canals, cremation, prohibition, and longevity. Cranioscopy continues, with the practical utility of anthropology in its psychic department. Creation's Mysteries prints communications from Hahnemann and Spurzheim, delivered through a trance medium, and tests them against psychometry. The journal reflects its editor's wide, unorthodox curiosity. The pages mix fact, faith, and fancy. The last notes treat spirit papers. The range is wide.
30266-tales-from-blackwood-volume-7:
Volume 7 of Tales from Blackwood gathers stories first printed in the Edinburgh magazine, published by William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London. Frederick Hardman opens with My English Acquaintance, from February 1848. A narrator at a Palais Royal coffee house meets a young sergeant of French light dragoons, smart in a green forage cap, who claims his acquaintance in perfect English. T. Doubleday follows with The Murderer's Last Night.

Later tales include a narration of uncommon things by Herbert Willis, a divinity graduate, plus The Wags, The Wet Wooing as a narrative of 1798, and Ben-na-Groich. The set shows Blackwood's range, from Paris encounters and crime to Irish history and Highland scenes. Readers of Victorian magazine fiction will find the volume a varied, brisk sample of Maga at work.
30976-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Held here is the prefatory matter of volume seven of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, running from Constantine Pavlovich to Demidov. It lists every edition from the first, in three volumes from 1768 to 1771. It runs through the ninth, in twenty-five volumes from 1875 to 1889, to the eleventh, in twenty-nine volumes from 1910 to 1911.

The tenth edition, it notes, was the ninth edition with eleven supplementary volumes, from 1902 to 1903. Copyright in countries subscribing to the Bern Convention rests with the Chancellor, Masters and Scholars of the University of Cambridge. The American copyright of 1910 rests with the Encyclopaedia Britannica Company of New York. A list of initials identifies individual contributors to volume seven. It is the front matter of a great reference work.
31134-stories-by-american-authors-volume:
Volume seven of Stories by American Authors, issued by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1896, collects six short stories by six writers. Octave Thanet opens with The Bishop's Vagabond, in which a widowed bishop strolls an April street in Aiken, greeting crowds of winter visitors and Southern townsfolk. Edward Bellamy follows with Lost, and Louise Stockton with Kirby's Coals of Fire.

Margaret Floyd, James T. McKay, and Virginia W. Johnson complete the set with a journal of a social wreck, Stella Grayland, and The Image of San Donato. The volume gives a compact sample of late nineteenth-century American magazine fiction, from clerical comedy to social satire and romance.
32622-st-nicholas-magazine-for-boys-and-:
St. Nicholas, an illustrated magazine for young folks conducted by Mary Mapes Dodge, volume thirteen, part two, May to October 1886, gathers stories, poems, jingles, and pictures for children. Its contents range from boat-building and fly-fishing for trout to stories of English painters and fishes and their young.

Verses include the Brownies at base-ball, at lawn tennis, in the menagerie, and on roller skates, alongside an ambitious kangaroo, a ballad of base-ball, and a captain's Fourth of July kite. Illustrated throughout, the volume shows a magazine that mixed instruction, humor, and adventure for young readers.
3853-memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-mo:
Madame de Montespan's seventh and last book follows the king's late wars and her own eclipse. Luxembourg falls because the king wills it, as Marshal de Crequi invests the town with thirty thousand men and takes it in a week. Treves follows, its fine fortifications leveled, while fire, pillage, and devastation spread through the electorate, since imperial forces stand far away against the Ottomans.

Portraits of Louvois, the dragonades, Meudon, and a horoscope fill the volume, with Madame de Maintenon advising delay on demolishing an offensive pyramid, lest scoffers call it part of a bargain. The king relishes the counsel, and court business goes on. Readers who reach this book will find Montespan watching an empire's glory curdle into ruin, with her own star long set.
4419-sandra-belloni-volume-7:
Book Seven of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni opens with Emilia locked up with her mother all one evening. The kind, sharp-voiced, untidy little woman helps try on dresses, runs about for pins, and gives her critical taste. The domestic scene precedes the novel's closing movements.

The book's chapters promise Emilia beginning to feel Merthyr's power, a chapter interrupted by the philosopher, and a fresh duet between Wilfrid and Emilia. Alderman's bouquet, the explosion at Brookfield, and the tragedy of sentiment follow, with frost on the May night and Emilia's goodbye. This final volume resolves Emilia's long trial.
4433-evan-harrington-volume-7:
Book Seven of George Meredith's Evan Harrington opens in the domain of tailordom, where peace reigns in Mr. Goren's shop. Harassed officials, ruined traders, and diplomatists with headaches might envy that peace over work well done. The shop, long a joke, becomes the center of attraction.

The book's chapters follow the countess still scenting game, an abominable plot of the brothers Cogglesby, and portraits of Juliana and Rose. A warning to all conspirators follows, with a lover's parting and a year later, when the countess writes to her sister Caroline. This final volume settles Evan's rank, love, and trade.
4441-vittoria-volume-7:
Book Seven of George Meredith's Vittoria returns to episodes of the revolt and the war, with Count Karl Lenkenstein, the story of the Guidascarpi, and the victory of the volunteers. The deeds of Barto Rizzo follow, with a meeting at Roveredo, and then the close of the Lombard campaign and Vittoria's perplexity.

Later chapters bring a fresh entanglement, a stay on Lago Maggiore, Violetta d'Isorella, and Anna of Lenkenstein. Vittoria the singer, caught between lover and cause, faces the revolution's aftermath. This volume carries the Italian struggle from battle toward the tangled peace that follows victory.
4450-the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-vo:
Book Seven of George Meredith's Adventures of Harry Richmond opens near a gravel pit heath, where a single tent stands in a gully by an iron-red rillet. A girl of Kiomi's tribe leans over the lazy water, striking it with her handkerchief, while a new carriage waits a stone's throw away. Gipsy life and grand life meet again.

The book's chapters promise within an inch of Harry's life, days among gipsy women, and his father acting the charmer again. The princess entrapped follows, with a general gathering and all caught in his father's net. An encounter showing his father's genius in a strong light closes the book, as the adventurer's schemes peak.
4459-beauchamp-s-career-volume-7:
Book Seven of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career opens at the cottage on the common, in the night, with a question of pilgrimage and an act of penance. The apology to Dr. Shrapnel follows, with its fruits, and chapters without love and the last of Nevil Beauchamp. The radical's career reaches its close.

Beauchamp, who fought elections, family, and his own passions for principle, ends in a quieter key. Meredith gives his hero penance rather than triumph, and love's absence rather than its reward. This final volume completes a political novel that refuses easy victory, and honors constancy over success.
5814-following-the-equator-a-journey-aro:
Part seven of Mark Twain's Following the Equator covers chapters sixty-one through sixty-nine, closing the world journey with reflection. A Pudd'nhead Wilson maxim jokes that God first made idiots for practice, then made school boards, and the chapter asks a pointed question. Suppose no more ingenuity went to teaching deaf, dumb, and blind children than sometimes goes to teaching American children with all their faculties intact?

Here Twain gives his late-journey meditations on education, empire, and human folly, sharpened by months of travel. The part favors argument and aphorism over new scenery, as Twain sums up what the voyage taught him. It suits readers finishing the book in order, and it offers a fitting, provocative close to a journey around the world.
5824-the-gilded-age-part-7:
Part seven of The Gilded Age, by Twain and Warner, covers chapters fifty-five through sixty-three, opening in a courtroom. Henry Brierly takes the stand, and at the district attorney's request he tells the jury all he knows about a killing, narrating circumstances readers already know in substance. He accompanied Miss Hawkins to New York at her request, supposing she came about a bill pending in Congress.

Readers reach the novel's trial and reckoning, as testimony, reputation, and Washington schemes collide in open court. The part turns satire grave, letting law weigh what lobbying and love have wrought. It suits readers finishing the Gilded Age, since the verdict here closes Laura's long arc and the novel's argument about gilded promises.
5842-sketches-new-and-old-part-7:
Part seven of Mark Twain's Sketches New and Old opens with a first interview with Artemus Ward, written about 1870. Twain had never seen Ward before, though Ward brought letters of introduction from mutual friends in San Francisco, and by invitation Twain breakfasted with him. In the silver mines, Twain notes, it was almost religion to precede such a meal with whisky cocktails.

Readers meet two great American humorists sizing each other up over breakfast, with frontier manners as the joke. The part gathers further late sketches, showing Twain's mature comic voice at ease. It suits readers who enjoy literary encounters, western humor, and Twain's habit of turning a simple meeting into a memorable story.
7139-the-great-conspiracy-volume-7:
Logan's seventh part of The Great Conspiracy opens at chapter twenty eight, Freedom at Last Assured, with a brief military survey. Hood had marched north with some 50,000 men toward Nashville. Sherman, leaving Thomas and some 35,000 men behind to thwart him, abandoned his base and marched south from Atlanta through Georgia toward the sea. On November 30, 1864, Schofield, commanding the Fourth and Twenty Third Corps of Thomas's army, stood at Franklin in the angle of the Harpeth River.

With fewer than 20,000 Union troops behind hasty works, Schofield met Hood's impetuous assault, at first threatening bloody rout, and turned it by brilliant counter charge and obstinate defense. The stand bought time for Union supply trains to cross the river. Only this seventh part's campaign is traced here, as freedom's assurance nears.
7160-the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-7:
Part seven of Twain's Prince and the Pauper opens at chapter twenty two, A Victim of Treachery, with King Foo foo the First roving again among tramps and outlaws. He serves as butt for coarse jests and dull witted railleries, sometimes victim of small spite at Canty's and Hugo's hands when the Ruffler's back turns. None but Canty and Hugo truly dislike him; some others like him, and all admire his pluck and spirit.

For two or three days Hugo, in whose ward the king stands, covertly makes the boy uncomfortable, and at nightly orgies amuses the company by small indignities offered as if by accident. Twice he steps upon the king's toes accidentally, and the king, as royalty demands, stays contemptuously unconscious and indifferent. The third time, the king fells Hugo to the ground with a cudgel, to the tribe's prodigious delight.
7199-the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-7:
Part Seven of Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer sets Tom and Huck to watch a tavern and its alley for a Spaniard who never comes. One boy watches the alley from a distance while the other minds the tavern door, and night after night the watch fails: clear skies, a closed tavern, and no stranger at all. Huck beds down in an empty sugar hogshead past midnight.

Thursday night promises better, and Tom slips out with his aunt's old tin lantern, blindfolded with a towel, to try the keys while Huck stands sentry. The long wait weighs on Huck like a mountain, and Tom's silence in the dark stretches into dread. This part holds the alley watch and its slow, comic suspense.
7248-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur:
Part Seven of Mark Twain's Connecticut Yankee opens with Dowley's humiliation, as a cargo arrives toward sunset on Saturday and the Yankee struggles to keep the Marcos from fainting. They blame themselves as accessories to ruin, sure that Jones and the Yankee are bankrupt past help, while the Yankee has bought far more than dinner stuff for the family's future comfort.

Wheat, rare as ice-cream to a hermit at tables of their class, a sizeable dinner table, and two whole pounds of salt count as wild extravagance in their eyes. Twain lets peasant thrift and Yankee plenty collide in a comic scene of fear and generosity. This part holds the cargo, the Marcos, and their terror at plenty.
8477-life-on-the-mississippi-part-7:
Part 7 of Life on the Mississippi opens with chapter 31, A Thumb-print and What Came of It, as Twain's boat approaches Napoleon, Arkansas. The time is noonday, bright and sunny, which troubles him, since his errand there is not, preferably, a noonday kind of errand. The more he thinks, the more the fact pushes itself upon him, in one form and another.

This section belongs to Twain's return journey, revisiting old river towns and settling old scores, with anecdotes piling up around a mysterious errand. Readers get the older Twain as traveler and storyteller, mixing memory, mischief, and observation. It is the book in its reminiscent vein, where every town holds a tale.
8588-roughing-it-part-7:
This seventh part of Mark Twain's Roughing It opens at chapter sixty-one with Dick Baker, a pocket-miner of Dead-House Gulch, worn down by eighteen years of unrewarded toil. Twain calls him grave, simple, and slouchily dressed, with a heart finer than any gold his shovel ever found. When luck runs against him, Baker mourns a wonderful cat he once owned. Since men without women or children nearby, Twain notes, take up with pets because they must love something.

The cat story, famous in its own right, grows into a tall tale of mining, mourning, and animal cunning. Around it sit more camp scenes of hope, failure, and stubborn endurance. The part shows Twain at his most affectionate toward frontier losers. It closes the book's long arc from greenhorn traveller to a man who understands what the West cost the people who stayed.
8707-the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-7:
Gustave Dore's seventh Bible volume follows Jesus through his ministry in Galilee and on the road to Jerusalem. It opens with Jesus walking on the water: the disciples toil at rowing against a contrary wind. In the fourth watch of the night he comes to them across the sea, calming their fear and the wind. Christ's entry into Jerusalem, the tribute money question, and the widow's mite follow.

Parables and miracles fill the later pages: raising the daughter of Jairus, the good Samaritan and his arrival at the inn. The prodigal son, Lazarus and the rich man, the Pharisee and the publican. Jesus with the woman of Samaria. The passages show teacher, healer, and storyteller in turn. Readers can use the volume as a gospel reader, moving from wonder to teaching in the order Dore chose to picture them.
9449-samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-:
Part seven of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren follows Samantha's fight to fund the women's fair work for the meeting house. The part opens with Josiah counting his cash: four fifty-dollar bills, a ten, and a five. Asked for fair money, he pockets the bills and hands his wife a ten-cent piece. Samantha's wrath, told in rich dialect, drives the comedy that follows.

Chapters track the women's toil, the men's tight fists, and Samantha's plain-spoken case for a fair share. The jokes bite, but the plea stays earnest: women's work deserves men's coin. A reader gets a late slice of Holley's long farm-wife saga, funny and pointed, with church funds as the battleground.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
Part 7 of Mark Twain's A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court opens at Marco's Sunday dinner. There Hank humiliates the boastful Dowley by comparing wages and prices across thirteen centuries. Talk of sixth-century political economy turns dangerous when the company's loyalty is questioned, the disguised king's temper betrays them, and both travellers fall into the hands of men happy to sell them.

Sold as slaves, Hank and Arthur are priced, marched, and put on the road in a gang, learning what a human being fetches in their own kingdom's market. One incident on the march, a young mother sold away from her child, is told without comedy at all. The part ends with the pair in London in chains, and Hank counting the hours to rescue or the gallows.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-7:
Lactantius leads volume seven of the Ante-Nicene Fathers, the Roberts and Donaldson set of 1885, which spans the third and fourth centuries. Around him stand Venantius, Asterius, and Victorinus, then Dionysius. The volume's back half turns from authors to documents: apostolic teaching and constitutions, a homily, and early liturgies.

Lactantius, called the Christian Cicero for his style, argues the faith to educated pagans. The Apostolic Constitutions then lay down church order in the apostles' borrowed names: how to baptize, ordain, and judge. The liturgies preserve some of the oldest Christian prayers we have. The volume shows doctrine hardening into institution.
arabian-nights-payne-1884-vol-7:
Payne's seventh volume of the Thousand Nights and One Night came out in 1884, as the nine-volume labor neared its end. Nights from the Calcutta edition unfold in John Payne's complete English, still unexpurgated. The great cycle's later tales grow reflective as often as wild, though wonders never cease for long.

Following the whole set volume by volume shows how the Nights built a world rather than a plot. Storytellers within stories keep the frame supple across hundreds of nights. Volume VII holds the late stretch of that world, two volumes short of the close Payne promised his first readers.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-7:
Michael L. Rodkinson's seventh Talmud volume gathers three tractates on holy days: Betzah, Moed Katan, and Succah. The set, in the 1918 edition, was the first full English Babylonian Talmud. Each tractate guards a different corner of the festival year.

Betzah sets what may be cooked and carried on a feast day. Moed Katan rules the in-between days of a festival: what work may be done, and how mourning fits a season of joy. Succah gives the law of the booth for the Feast of Tabernacles, its walls, its roof of branches, and the four kinds of plants waved in prayer. Together they show festival law at its most practical.
bancroft-history-us-vol-7:
Yorktown crowns the seventh volume of Bancroft's History of the United States, issued in the eighteen fifties. The war's endgame brings siege, surrender, and hard talks for peace. American independence, so long a hope, stands won and secured at last.

Bancroft brings his main narrative to its first great climax here. A young republic faces the world as an equal of empires. He lingers on the joy and relief of a people delivered. The volume closes the war story of his epic. The harder task of building a nation fills the volumes that follow it in time.
beauchamp-s-career-volume-7:
Volume seven closes George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career, from chapter fifty to fifty-six. Lord Romfrey rides through rain to Dr. Shrapnel's cottage on the common. The old radical lies hurt after the attack that shamed the family. A question of pilgrimage and an act of penance frame the Earl's errand.

The apology to Dr. Shrapnel is at last delivered, too late for easy peace. Without Love and The Last of Nevil Beauchamp end the story with Nevil's death. Meredith gathers his themes of heroism, class pride, and wasted ardour in a sombre close. The radical sailor who would not compromise is mourned by friends who never followed him. Readers finish one of the most ambitious political novels of the Victorian age.
captain-rogers-the-lady-of-the-barge-and:
W. W. Jacobs wrote a set of tales fronted by The Lady of the Barge, and this part holds the tale Captain Rogers. A tired man comes over an old stone bridge at the start. Dark river and still craft sit to one side, best not eyed. Town lights on the far bank draw his gaze with more cheer.

His hose are darned and holed, his coat and knee breeches worn rusty. Far miles show in his forced step. At bridge end he pulls tall and steps brave to the inn row. Queen Anne beershop gets no pause. Royal George and Trusty Anchor get one glance each. The Golden Key, best house in Riverstone and the gentry's choice, takes him in. A faded coat squared with a swagger marks the man the tale will test.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100030002-7:
Self-assessment packet for CIA personnel officers is dated October 1979 and marked Administrative, Internal Use Only. A covering memorandum from Harry E. Fitzwater, Director of Personnel, asks every personnel officer to take part. He recalls a first self-assessment held during the fall of 1976.

The effort was designed to give Office of Personnel management information about officers' capabilities and interests as personnel careerists, the memo states. It would show where action was needed to keep the Office able to meet its varied duties. Completed questionnaires were due back no later than 9 November 1979. The numbered items ask officers to rate their own knowledge and skill across the trade. They cover mobilization planning, statistical methods, and grade and ceiling controls. One item covers working out travel, living, and office costs for employees under nonofficial cover.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100040001-7:
Memorandum DD/A 81-1667/1 from Harry E. Fitzwater, Deputy Director for Administration, forwards a consultants' report on the agency's psychological activities. Addressees include the heads of the National Foreign Assessment Center, Operations, and Science and Technology. The Inspector General and the Director of Medical Services also received it.

The report itself, titled Psychologists in the Central Intelligence Agency, was completed on 22 October 1981. Its covering letter of 23 October thanks the men and women who furnished written material and shared observations. Two issues get a further word: how to assure quality control of psychological work, and how to improve contact among psychologists. Fitzwater asked for written comments by close of business 29 October, to meet a deadline set by the Deputy Director. The report states the Psychological Services Division screened, through testing and assessment, about 70 percent of professional candidates for agency jobs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100130010-7:
Appendix 1, marked for internal use only, examines the validity and reliability of PATB in depth. To judge the evidence, its authors reviewed 23 studies done by or under the Psychological Services Staff. They also used the Test Data Book Number 15 of 1 July 1958, and held a one-day conference with the staff chief and his team.

Early on they found that not all applicants for professional posts had to take the battery. No written policy said who was exempt, they report. Some exceptions looked sound, such as specialists recruited for knowledge the battery never tested. But candidates with like schooling and experience, chasing the same job in the same unit, were treated differently, they found. That did not seem reasonable, they write. On results, links between battery scores and job performance ratings were uneven across job groups. What consistency existed sat in the thinking tests.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100020003-7:
Memorandum for the record, dated 12 June 1981 and marked Secret, inventories a History Staff holding coded MISC-18. It is Donovan and CIA, a history of the establishment of the Central Intelligence Agency, dating to 1975. The history was never published nor listed as finished, the memo states.

It nevertheless looks ready for the Historical Series, the memo notes. Two spiral-bound volumes hold 792 pages, with illustrations and a complete table of contents. A note places the set in a Conservafile in the vault, third shelf from the top. The attached contents open with a prewar part on the COI story. Chapters cover the intelligence services of 1929 to 1939 and G-2 and ONI on the eve of war. A second part profiles Colonel William J. Donovan, from his early years through his work as Roosevelt's emissary in 1940. Later sections trace his clashes with the Joint Chiefs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100020049-7:
Letter of 13 March 1981 from Roberta S. Knapp, Acting Chief of the Historical Staff, answers Professor Donald Coers of Sam Houston State University. His letter to Director William Casey had been referred to her office. Coers was researching John Steinbeck, and a claimed meeting with William Donovan.

An official familiar with the Donovan papers had no memory of any reference to such a meeting, Knapp writes. The summer and early fall of 1941 were a time of intense organising as the Coordinator of Information got underway, she allows, so some contact would have a certain logic. The bulk of the Donovan papers, about 110 boxes, sat at the US Army Military History Institute at Carlisle Barracks, she advises. Donovan's biographer Anthony Cade Brown reportedly held exclusive access to them through 1982. The incoming letter, quoted below, traces the claim to critic Lewis Gannett on Steinbeck's novel The Moon Is Down.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100040092-7:
Korean War papers held by the CIA are the subject of a memorandum dated 12 May 1982, sent to the Director of the Foreign Broadcast Information Service. The Army Center of Military History had asked for access for Albert Cowdrey, who was researching an official Army medical history volume. His topic was Communist propaganda charges of germ warfare in 1950 to 1953.

A computer search of Agency holdings had turned up a set of papers matching the topic. Three of them are enclosed and the addressee is asked to rule on whether Cowdrey may use them. Any material released still needed Agency review before it could be downgraded or printed, under the access policy the memo cites.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01m00147r000100350002-7:
National Security Directive 34, Partnership with Panama, is an action plan to foster economic recovery, dated 24 January 1990. Routing slips send the paper to the Director and the Latin America analysis and operations offices. The plan is addressed to the Vice President and a long list of cabinet and agency heads.

The plan holds that private initiative, backed by Panamanian reform, is the key to recovery. First comes a 42 million dollar aid program run by the Agency for International Development. It covers replacement housing for the Chorillo area, emergency public works, and help for small firms hurt by looting. Next, the Export-Import Bank would offer up to 400 million dollars in guarantees to finance sales of American goods.
cia-crest-cia-rdp03t02547r000100220001-7:
Honduran armed forces are assessed in a secret intelligence paper dated October 1981, from the National Foreign Assessment Center. Its title pairs military capabilities with political role. The paper rests on information available as of 30 September 1981, and it was coordinated with several analysis offices and the operations directorate.

Findings in the body are blunt about weak spots. Eight patrol boats must cover the Gulf of Fonseca and a long north coast, yet they need major overhaul and carry no radar or heavy arms. Air-to-sea coordination is described as almost nonexistent, and communications gear and training as outdated. The army also lacks an effective reserve call-up and a real border patrol against arms infiltration.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100050001-7:
Events touching Cuba through one year are listed in a confidential reference aid dated April 1984, ALA 84-10024. Titled Cuban Chronology 1983, it comes from the Directorate of Intelligence. The preface says the listing covers major domestic and international events affecting Cuba from 1 January to 31 December 1983.

Entries are arranged alphabetically by country, with two extra subject groupings for the Nonaligned Movement and the Palestine Liberation Movement. The preface is plain that the selection is not complete: events were picked for their own weight. Sample pages track visits, ambassador appointments, and talks, such as a Cuban parliamentary trip through Algeria and Kuwait in January. A key to abbreviations opens the aid.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100230001-7:
Chile's banned but active political parties are examined in a secret intelligence assessment dated November 1984, ALA 84-10110. The paper came from the Latin American analysis office with help from the Office of Central Reference. Coordination with the operations directorate is noted on the title pages.

The opening reports that, despite legal proscription, Chile's parties play a large part in opposition to President Pinochet's eleven-year military-led regime. In practice, the government tolerated open activity by all but Marxist parties. Party histories follow: the National Party dissolved itself in 1973 in support of the new regime, while the Christian Democrats kept a largely underground structure. Their later calls for consensus and moderation are weighed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100410001-7:
Colombia's crackdown on drug trafficking is reported in a memorandum dated 3 October 1984. South America and international security analysts shared the work, coordinated with the operations directorate. It rests on information available as of 12 September 1984 and carries the number ALA-M-84-10099.

Evidence tying traffickers to the killing of Justice Minister Lara the previous spring pushed President Betancur into hard steps. He declared a state of siege, brought the armed forces into the campaign, and allowed military courts for accused traffickers. He also agreed to work the extradition treaty with the United States and backed a pilot marijuana spraying program. The paper reports that networks were briefly paralyzed and some traffickers fled abroad.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000301840001-7:
Japan's special tax incentives for industry are traced in a memorandum resting on information available as of 3 July 1984. The Japan Branch prepared the paper. Its theme is decline: a tool once used to target favored industries has weakened as budgets tightened and more groups gained a voice in tax policy.

Incentives fell from over 6 percent of corporate tax collections in the years 1965 to 1975 to under 3 percent last year, the paper reports. In the late 1950s and 1960s the benefits aimed to make basic materials and manufacturing firms fit for world markets. Later measures spread across wider national aims. A robot and electronics tax credit for small firms is one example given.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100150001-7:
Possible successors to Paraguay's president are profiled in a secret research paper dated August 1985, CR 85-14144. The Office of Central Reference and the Latin American analysis office shared the work, coordinated with the operations directorate. It rests on information available as of 15 July 1985.

Although 72-year-old President Alfredo Stroessner is not expected to leave office soon, the paper reports that political infighting is growing sharper. Candidate profiles follow. One covers a ruling party secretary disliked by key military figures, including General Rodriguez. Another covers Abdo Benitez, 57, a party secretary with strength among party youth that worries traditionalists. Each profile weighs party posts held and ground lost or kept.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100330001-7:
Fidel Castro's absence from a Soviet leader's funeral is read as a snub in a memorandum dated 28 March 1985. The State Department's Cuban affairs director requested the paper, and Latin American analysts prepared it. The funeral was that of Soviet General Secretary Konstantin Chernenko, held on 13 March.

The paper judges that Castro meant to show his unhappiness with parts of Soviet policy. Grievances listed include slower Soviet oil deliveries, pressure for economic austerity in Cuba, and weak Soviet engagement in Central America and Africa. Skipping a first meeting with Gorbachev suggests little hope of near-term improvement, the paper says. The basic relationship, though, is not seen as threatened.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000200780001-7:
Japan's high savings rate is questioned in a secret research paper dated May 1985, EA 85-10098. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it, using information available as of 10 May 1985. Its title asks whether Japan will kick the high savings habit.

American calls to cut or better use Japanese savings at home have struck a raw nerve in Tokyo, the summary reports. Even Japanese backers of fiscal stimulus insist in public that savings choices are purely internal. The body weighs two opposing forces that will settle the rate: the age spread of the population and where financial assets sit by age. Data limits keep the paper from drawing a firm parallel with the American savings fall.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201400001-7:
A proposed tax on Japanese exports splits the government in a memorandum dated 22 March 1985. The Japan Branch prepared the paper, using information available that day. It carries the number EA M 85-10054.

Some officials want an export tax to narrow the huge trade surplus and head off an American import surcharge. The Ministry of Finance, which holds the legal power to set such a tax, opposes the move. Other arms of the state take the surcharge threat more gravely: the trade and industry ministry, the Foreign Ministry, and the Economic Planning Agency are named as most concerned. In public, senior officials keep quiet or play down how near American action may be.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201680001-7:
China's national political scene in a tense spring is drawn in a memorandum dated 6 June 1985. Reformers led by Deng Xiaoping push a reluctant bureaucracy forward on a broad agenda, the summary reports. Policies passed last year have sped growth but also bred economic and political trouble.

Midlevel officials resist streamlining and renewal moves that threaten their posts and perks. A party conference set for September forms a self-set deadline for major changes in national and provincial leadership. The paper reads the fight as one inside the reform camp, between elders and younger technocrats, not a bid to topple Deng. Succession runs through it all: Deng, at 80, means to hand full power on.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000301850001-7:
China's fast growth and the strain it brings are covered in a memorandum dated 21 June 1985. Official Chinese figures put first-quarter industrial output 23 percent above the same period last year. Income and investment surges, plus reform-driven changes in production, drive the rise, the paper reports.

Officials welcome growth as proof that industrial reforms work, yet fear it will deepen shortages of energy and raw materials, strain transport, and feed inflation. Beijing mixes administrative steps with Western-style macro tools to cool the economy. The paper doubts that China's economic managers, new to a decentralized system and pressed by local hunger for quick results, can keep the control they hope for.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000301940001-7:
Next year's Tokyo Economic Summit and its pull on Japanese policy fill a memorandum dated 22 July 1985, EA M 85-10138. The Japan Branch prepared the paper, using information available that day. A duplicate file note is part of the released copy.

Tokyo's early start on hosting points to a hard push by Prime Minister Nakasone for a smooth meeting, the summary reports. His Paris trip this month aimed in part to talk President Mitterrand out of a boycott threat. Nakasone's term ends soon after the summit. The paper lists his stakes: a mark on foreign policy, a hand in choosing his successor, and a role behind the scenes after he steps down.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302020001-7:
Low American semiconductor sales to Japan are explained in a memorandum dated 31 July 1985, EA M 85-10149. The Japan Branch prepared the paper, using information available that day. American makers hold a smaller market share in Japan than elsewhere and blame protection.

Past limits on foreign access and structural factors explain the gap better than current trade barriers, the analysis finds. Until the mid-1970s, Japanese policy held back imports and foreign investment in electronics. The paper judges that the after-effects of those rules may still depress the American share. Market factors of today, though, play the larger role in holding sales down.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302200001-7:
A new index for tracking the Philippine economy is presented in a typescript memorandum dated 25 October 1985. Islands Branch and systems staff in the East Asian office built the work together. Current analysis suffers because data arrive three to six months late and face large revisions, the summary explains.

The CIA index follows money, prices, trade, profit expectations, government revenue, and factory jobs and costs. It is meant to give early warning of a turn in the economy, months before output figures appear. The latest reading suggests that a two-year decline has leveled off. Growth in exports, share prices, and reserve money in coming months would signal a real recovery; flat readings would warn of more malaise.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000100040015-7:
Comments on a Bar Association letter move through the administration directorate in a routing sheet dated 26 January 1984. Harry Fitzwater, Deputy Director for Administration, passes the file to the Associate General Counsel. The reference is a General Counsel memorandum of that month on the Bar questionnaire about intelligence oversight.

Fitzwater says he asked a colleague to review the memorandum and Frederick Hitz's questions. He finds the comments sensible and asks that the General Counsel and Stanley Sporkin give them consideration. Attached is a note from the Director of Information Services to Fitzwater, offering observations on the Hitz letter. Its first point remarks on the memorandum that transmitted the Bar letter itself.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000100070003-7:
Draft criminal law on defense information leaks is circulated in a file opened by a 16 January 1984 memorandum from the General Counsel's office. The memo tells a working group on intelligence requirements that Mr. Martin's report will be on the agenda for a meeting on 23 January. A re-draft by Mr. Clarke is also expected for discussion.

Thomas Martin of the Jenner and Block law firm sent the draft on 11 January 1984. His letter encloses proposed legislation and an advisory note for the task force. The draft bill would amend the National Security Act of 1947. Its title states the aim: prohibiting the unauthorized disclosure of restricted defense information.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000200460009-7:
A court opinion in United States v. Heine, cited as 151 F.2d 813, is reproduced in a Federal Reporter excerpt held in Agency files. The two-column printing is rough, and lines from a medical report in a neighboring case bleed into the scan. The Heine text itself concerns the Espionage Act.

The opinion defines the phrase information relating to the national defense. It holds that the phrase does not cover information lawfully open to everyone. The defendant, a German-born American citizen, had gathered all available material on American aircraft production. His aim was that Germany should be advised of American defense strength in the event of war. Factory locations, capacity, and worker numbers were among the details he sought.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200500008-7:
A newspaper commentary on Iran, with a note of praise pinned to it, makes up a January 1979 file. The clipping is the Christian Science Monitor of Wednesday 3 January 1979, opinion page. Its headline reads US in Iran: ignoring the facts. A typed note at the front calls it a great article.

The note says the piece tells one major reason American intelligence is often surprised: stress on current intelligence from classified documents, while long-range trends that need no secrets go ignored. The column itself argues that the White House shock at the Shah's weakness was a failure of political perception more than of intelligence. Open sources, it holds, already showed how badly things went.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200500017-7:
Vincent Davis passes on a contact suggestion in a letter to Stansfield Turner dated 21 October 1978. The letter fits Turner's wish for more open, friendly contact with the academic community. A scholar named in the letter, his name withheld in the release, wants two unclassified Agency publication series.

The series are the Economic Indicators Weekly Review and the International Energy Statistical Review, both issued by the national foreign assessment center. Davis also suggests a personal meeting, either in Washington or in Seattle. The man is described as a senior hand on fisheries problems who spent more of his life in government service, at the State Department, than in academic work. Warmth and hospitality are praised.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200500026-7:
Stansfield Turner sets out a shopping list of summer projects for Vincent Davis in a letter dated 30 May 1978. The letter is Turner's, though the catalog line reverses the names. He thanks Davis for a note of 9 May and reports that a staffer named Bob is back at work full-time, plugging along on one and a half eyes.

Turner is weighing how best to use Davis's talent during a brief summer stint. First comes the charter legislation task force under General Counsel Tony Lapham, deep in talks on Title I. Turner is frustrated at its failure to draw principles out of details, and wants help. Reorganization work, with new staff bodies for resource management, follows on the list.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000300830010-7:
An open hearing on intelligence charter legislation, held on 11 July 1978, is reported in a memorandum dated 14 July 1978, OLC 78-0399/94. The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence heard three witnesses billed as victims of past intelligence abuses. Attendance by senators was the poorest yet: only Senator Garn sat through it.

The witnesses were Louis Schneider of the American Friends Service Committee, Ethel Taylor for Women Strike for Peace, and Richard Gutman of a Chicago project on political surveillance litigation. Schneider stressed his committee's support for the letter and spirit of the First Amendment. His testimony opposed the continuation of secret activities of the kind his group had faced. Brief sketches of each organization are attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401040006-7:
DCI Schedules, December 1977 opens with a topic index of the Director's actions. The headings are analysis, cover, and defense. Executive Order 12036 and the Middle East appear too. So do national-tactical issues, paramilitary matters, personnel, and security. The entries include a meeting with the Joint Chiefs. That meeting dealt with the national-tactical interface. Phone talks with the President and Dr. Brzezinski are listed. They dealt with the wording of the executive order. Memos on detailees and security also appear.

The daily pages record an OMB budget review. They record a mini-Policy Review Committee meeting. A Department of Defense counterintelligence briefing appears. So do discussions of estimate NIE 3/3. Phone logs name callers such as Deputy Secretary Duncan and Dr. Brzezinski. Redactions are scattered through the copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401180001-7:
Business Council, Homestead, Virginia, 13-14 May 1977 is represented here by one memo. The memo for the record is dated 18 May 1977. Its title is "Business Council Thoughts." It records impressions Turner carried away from the meeting. It notes Joe Califano's view on social security. In that view, business could pick up a billion dollars of the tab. The businessmen answered that added taxes simply become higher prices.

The memo also records Russell Long's remarks on the power of the press. Long spoke of members of Congress beholden to the press as well. The memo names the Business Roundtable as a parallel channel to government. It names the National Association of Businessmen the same way. It notes the next meeting's dates, 13-15 October at the Homestead. Robert Hatfield of Continental was program chairman.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601460017-7:
Wayne Reynolds wrote to Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, on 15 November 1977 from the Golden Plate Awards Council. He wrote as coordinator for Golden Plate invitations. On behalf of named judges and generals, he thanks Turner for taking the Academy's invitation. The Academy of Achievement wished to honor him at its banquet.

Turner's reply sits in the same file. He accepts with pleasure, he writes. He and Mrs Turner would try to attend the full run of events. The banquet itself was certain, he adds. His staff would firm up the details. The council roster on the letterhead names past award winners from many fields.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601460026-7:
Banquet progress report number 6 tracks the 1978 Golden Plate awards. The Academy of Achievement issued these reports as the event drew near. Much of the text gives short lives of the year's honorees. A hockey star's marks fill one sketch: most goals, most assists and most points in his sport.

A young singer gets a sketch drawn from press praise. A flight crew member is honored for bravery in the Canary Islands crash, where 581 persons died. She crawled from a burning plane with a broken arm and helped others. The report, kept in Central Intelligence Agency files, shows how the Academy built up its guests before the June banquet.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601460035-7:
Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, wrote to Howard N Kay on 16 March 1978 with a glad yes. Kay commanded the Naval Education and Training Center at Newport. Turner says he will be pleased to speak at Kay's change of command and retirement rite. It is hard to think of Kay leaving, he adds.

A staff note of 8 March 1978 sits with the letter. The note records that Kay called that day. Turner's acceptance was passed on by phone. Kay asked if Turner would come on the morning of the 22nd or the night before. The file ties the Newport rite to the Kentucky trip planned for the same June days.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601460044-7:
Messenger Inquirer of Owensboro makes up this Central Intelligence Agency file as a full day's paper. It is dated Saturday, June 24, 1978 and priced at fifteen cents. A photo on the front shows Colonel Harland Sanders meeting jockey Steve Cauthen for the first time. The meeting took place at a picnic for Academy of Achievement guests.

Local news leads the rest of the front page. A jury in a murder trial of a past city detective hung after long hours of talk. Court and zoning fights fill other columns. The paper covers the same awards weekend as the Louisville file. It shows the host town's own view of its big weekend.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601470016-7:
Notes from the Aspen Institute workshop fill this Central Intelligence Agency file in day order. The workshop ran from 24 to 28 July 1978. Its theme was secrecy, national security and rule in an open society. Monday notes record Harlan Cleveland on openness and secrecy. Moral choices rest with persons, not with bodies, he argued.

A test runs through his talk: would the act feel right under public gaze? Later notes take up Graham Allison on the case for secrecy in running a state. Good rule needs informed debate, the notes say. The file is a working record of what was said, kept by a hand at the talks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601480015-7:
Barron's Profiles of American Colleges supplies this excerpt on the University of Kentucky. A routing slip from the agency sits at the front. The pages come from the 1976 edition of the guide. They set out how the school takes in new students, with figures on applications and offers.

About 440 of 494 applicants were taken in one year, the entry says. Some 235 freshmen enrolled. Many ranked in the top fifth of their high school class. Notes cover aid, fees paid in parts, and the date by which honor scholarship bids should be filed. The file is reference matter kept for a Kentucky trip that spring.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601480024-7:
Turner wrote to Vincent Davis on 24 August 1977 about a WORLDVIEW 78 plan. He thanks Davis for the proposal, then pushes back. The plan would overdo his part, he suggests. His bent is for a low-key approach to campus life, as Davis had first urged.

A talk to a high school audience might play badly in the press, he adds. He is loath to pull top agency staff away for two days as resource people. His counter offer is plain: a lecture or two at a time that suits, lunch with the Rotarians, and something on campus. The letter shows a new director rationing his public face.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601500012-7:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) scheduling item number 78-072 logs a Business Council meeting. The item was received on 29 March 1978. The event ran from 11 to 13 May 1978, a Thursday through Saturday. The place was The Homestead at Hot Springs, Virginia. John W Burke Jr sent the invitation by letter.

A suspense date of 7 April is marked on the form. The Vice President was invited as Friday dinner speaker. Mrs Turner was invited too. The form carries spaces for the director's decision and for passing the item to deputies. It is a plain staff sheet, but it shows how each ask on the director's time was logged and judged.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601510011-7:
Annual report for 1976 of the Aerospace Industries Association fills this file. The opening pages list the officers of the association. S N McDonnell chairs the board. Karl G Harr Jr serves as president. Vice presidents cover fields from law to research and technology.

An executive committee roll follows, drawn from the great plane and engine firms. Boeing, IBM and Singer men sit on it. The report proper then covers the trade's year. The book gives the aerospace world in the trade's own account: its firms, its chiefs and its concerns.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100040003-7:
Administration of the oath of office to Admiral Turner fills this transcript. The rite took place on 9 March 1977 in the Headquarters Auditorium. Mr Knoche opens the day with a welcome to the President, Justice White and the guests. Turner would be the 12th Director of Central Intelligence, he notes.

Justice Byron White gave the oath, with Turner repeating the words. The President then addressed the crowd of cabinet members, Congress members and spy staff. The file is the full record of a change at the top. It marks the formal start of Turner's tenure at the agency, sworn in before the house he would lead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100090017-7:
Report of the Management Advisory Group covers fifteen months in this file. A memo dated 14 October 1977 sends it to the Director of Central Intelligence. The period runs from 1 July 1976 to 30 September 1977. Each issue the group acted on is listed in time order, not by theme. Annexes hold the papers behind each item.

Career planning draws sharp words in the body. Staff cannot plan careers alone, the group argues. Management must share that task as a joint endeavor. No new systems are needed, it says. The ones on hand should be used well. The report is the ranks' own audit of how the house was run.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100170009-7:
Recruitment process fills this memo from the Director of Personnel. Harry E Fitzwater signs it, from the policy, planning and management office. The memo goes to the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence. Two earlier memos frame it: one from August 1980 and an interim report from September 1980.

Those memos flow from a finding in an inspector general report on recruitment. Finding number 42 is named in the references. Status reports on problems and progress under the new hiring system were requested. This memo is the next such report. The file shows hiring treated as a system to be fixed, with grades, delays and processing all under watch.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200560032-7:
Bob Keating wrote on December 8, 1978 with thoughts on Zaire. He had enjoyed a train conversation with Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence,. Turner had asked for his views in writing. United States policy is to help steady Zaire in politics and trade, Keating notes. Large sums would flow over three years.

Aid and investment programs would carry much of the money. An IMF stabilization program of one billion dollars stands beside them. Keating doubts the recovery path as drawn. His years in Zaire and knowledge of aid work shape the doubt. The letter is a field man's warning: money alone would not fix the Zaire economy as planned.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200650014-7:
Director of Central Intelligence meeting with the Administration Management Advisory Group gets an agenda dated 7 March 1978. Topic one is follow-up remarks by the DCI on personnel flow-through. It refers back to a meeting of 27 May 1977. Ten minutes are allowed for it. General discussion takes twenty minutes next.

Problems in communications get ten minutes. Agency stability gets ten more. The body of the file expands each topic in turn. Flow-through is traced through an advisory group memo sent after the May meeting. The agenda shows the director in set session with his own managers, working a list of house problems by the clock.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200680011-7:
Director of Central Intelligence meeting with student trainees gets an agenda for 1 September 1977. The trainees are co-op students in the house. Topic one is internal problems, at ten minutes. Intelligence community problems take fifteen. Outreach takes ten, and the student training program fifteen.

An addendum fills the last ten minutes. Under internal problems, low morale leads. Disillusionment runs outside and inside the agency, the paper says. Talk of layoffs and reshaping feeds it. Poor communication and the isolation of the director's office are named too. The agenda shows the youngest staff in the house given a frank hour with its chief.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200730006-7:
Managing the improvement of intelligence analysis fills a memo of 8 February 1979. It goes to the Director of Central Intelligence. A revised draft goes with the cover note. The draft was sanitized for wider sharing, the writer says. Sanitizing kept it from insulting too many people without need.

Some specifics were suppressed in that cleaning. The director's own copy carries notes to recall them. The body then sets out management goals for analytic work. The file shows quality treated as a management problem: how to hire, train, task and judge the men and women who turn raw facts into assessments for the top.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200740005-7:
Program Corporation of America speakers catalog fills this thick file. It is a supplementary catalog to the firm's main book. Names on the covers give a partial list of the stars on offer. Dr Ralph Abernathy and Bella Abzug lead the roll in this copy. Steve Allen, Alan Arkin and Arthur Ashe follow.

Senators, professors and stage names crowd the list. The firm invites readers to ask for the general catalog by reply card. A program consultant could give more facts on any act. The file is a speaker bureau's wares, kept in the Director of Central Intelligence's office as a source for events and guests in that era.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200770002-7:
Part III of Executive Order 11905 rides in this file with a staff note on top. The note answers a question from Admiral Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence,. He had asked when the bar on assassination was set. President Ford's order forbade political assassination in plain words, the note says. A clip at page 31 shows the passage.

The order itself is dated February 18, 1976. Its title is United States Foreign Intelligence Activities. Contents and text fill the rest of the file. The pairing is telling: a director checks the exact birth of a ban that bound his own service, and staff answer with the text itself, marked to the page.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200780001-7:
Executive Order 12036 is explained to staff again in this copy of the director's notes. The note is No 21, dated 2 February 1978. President Carter signed the order on 24 January, Turner writes. It had been much on their minds for months. It shapes the intelligence structure, he says, and guides all facets of the work.

Three cardinal features carry weight for the agency, he argues. Policy makers at the top will now help set what gets gathered. They will tie those tasks to resources. They will review the end product too. The note is the director's own briefing of his house on the charter under which it would work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300820005-7:
Business Council letterhead opens this file from John W Burke Jr. Burke was executive secretary of the council. John D deButts chaired it. Vice chairmen named on the sheet include Benjamin F Biaggini, Robert S Hatfield, Thomas A Murphy and Irving S Shapiro. A roll of active members follows.

Chiefs of banks, phone firms and car makers fill the member list. The council sat on Seventeenth Street in Washington. Its letters went out under this formal head. The file is council correspondence to the Director of Central Intelligence, of the kind that carried invitations and meeting paper between the business world and the spy chief in those years.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300860001-7:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) trip to Pascagoula and Boca Raton fills this book for 9 to 12 March 1979. A contents page maps the pack. Schedule and points of contact lead. A commissioning program and procedure follow. Platform guests, a copy of the DCI's remarks and the status of shipbuilding at Pascagoula all have parts.

General information on the American College of Trial Lawyers and the Boca Raton Hotel closes the book. The schedule opens Friday 9 March with a 1430 departure. A John Hancock reception at the Longfellow House ends that day. Saturday brings Ingalls Shipbuilding and a commissioning. The book is a full trip brief in one binding.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301030001-7:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) trip to Principia College gets a schedule memo dated 4 February 1980. A special assistant to the DCI sends it to a distribution list. The trip covers Elsah, Illinois and Minneapolis, Minnesota. Dates are 5 to 7 February 1980. Tuesday 5 February opens with a run to Charlottesville, Virginia.

Times fill the day in the set form: arrivals, drives and evening events by the hour. Principia sits at Elsah, on the Mississippi bluffs. The memo is the staff plan for the college visit. It shows the director's travel run as a timed sheet, with each leg and stop entered before the party set out.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301070007-7:
United Technologies Corporation briefing notes fill this Central Intelligence Agency file for 26 June 1980. The slot ran from 1300 to 1430 on that Thursday. A B version is marked on the sheet. The notes open with a bond: both sides work in the risk assessment business. New ventures abroad are the firm's side of it.

The speaker would give his assessment of conditions overseas. An economic and political outlook leads. OPEC oil rose 125 percent in 1979, the notes stress. Tight policies to stem inflation come next. Elections in Japan and the United States are listed as key forces. The sheet is a talk outline for an industry audience.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401130036-7:
DCI scheduling item logs a speaking ask from Perry R Williams, dean of Trinity Cathedral in Cleveland. The item was received on 21 November 1979. Williams wrote from East 22nd Street. The ask was for a guest speaker spot with the Forum Committee of the City Club of Cleveland. Dates offered ran across Fridays in the new year: 18 or 25 January, any Friday in February except the 8th, and Fridays beyond.

The form leaves the choice open among those dates. Such items let the director's staff weigh one ask against a crowded diary. The file is the staff sheet for a churchman's invitation, kept with the letter that brought it to the agency that winter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401140035-7: Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) scheduling item 80-44 logs an award presentation for Thursday 20 March 1980. A letter from Bertrand M Harding brought the item, received on 22 February. The event would present a national Civil Service League career service award to John Waller. The hour was 1100. The place was the United States Civil Service Commission. A suspense date of 27 February is marked on the single-page form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401140044-7:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) routing and transmittal slip dated 22 February 1980 moves a speaking request in this file. The slip goes to the executive secretary. A remark on it is blunt: the DCI wants to regret on this speaking request. The letter in the file extends an invitation to the DCI or another speaker. Robert C Conolly II sent the invitation.

Slips like this one carried the office's verdicts. Boxes on the form offer the whole range of actions: file, clear, reply, circulate, comment. Here the action was a polite no, entered by hand. The file shows how a refusal moved: a letter in, a slip marked, and a reply prepared for the host.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401140053-7: An invitation form for the Director of Central Intelligence invitation form 80-26 logs a reception and dinner for Tuesday 4 March 1980. A letter from Howard E Vander Clute Jr brought it, received on 31 January. The evening would honor members of Congress. Congressman G V Montgomery would receive a Veterans of Foreign Wars congressional award. A suspense date of 7 February is marked on the single-page form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401150016-7: Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) invitation form 80-113 logs a tennis night for Tuesday 13 May 1980. A card brought the invitation, received on 21 April. The event was the eighth annual informal doubles round robin tennis tournament. Bill Lilley, a CBS vice president in Washington, hosted it. Hours were 1900 to 2300. The place was the Arlington Y Tennis and Squash Club on North 13th Street in Arlington, Virginia.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401150034-7:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) invitation form 80-97 logs a named lecture for Wednesday 16 April 1980. An invitation card brought it, received on 7 April 1980. The event was the Admiral Raymond Spruance Lecture at the Naval War College. Herman Wouk would give the lecture. Its title was Sadness and Hope: Some Thoughts on Modern Warfare.

The hour was 2000 at the Naval War College. The file is the staff sheet for a literary evening in a naval hall. A novelist of war at sea would lecture officers on war itself. The director's presence was sought as a guest of the college that spring.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401160015-7: A scheduling item for the Director of Central Intelligence scheduling item 80-162 logs an open-ended invitation from Roy Knauft Jr. A letter and a phone call from Santa Ana brought it. The ask was for an address by the DCI to the World Affairs Council of Orange County. No date was fixed. Santa Ana, California is the place named. A suspense date of 27 June 1980 is marked on the single-page form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401160042-7: Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) scheduling item 80-136 logs a seminar address for Friday 30 May 1980. A letter from Rabbi David Saperstein brought the item, received on 9 May. The seminar treated Washington perceptions of the Soviet threat. An interreligious staff council was the audience. The DCI would address it at 0945 hours in Washington. A suspense date of 15 May is marked on the single-page form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401310009-7:
Professional intelligence officer education gets a memorandum dated 16 May 1980. Robert Gates writes to the Director of Central Intelligence. Attached is a proposed outline of an educational program. The program would serve professional intelligence officers across the service. Two parts make up the outline, Gates notes.

A concept paper spells out the approach in broad terms. A general curriculum follows it. The aim is a shared schooling for a trade that had grown by apprenticeship. The file shows a young staff officer's hand in the design: Gates, later a director himself in the line of work, setting out how spies should be taught their profession.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501360003-7:
Press clippings for the week of 15 March fill this file. A Washington Star piece of 13 March 1980 leads the sampled pages. Carter backed on CIA secrecy is its head. The President's stand on guarding spy facts drew support in that report. Charter business fills much of the week around it.

The file is one week of a running story. Congress weighed the charter bills; the White House weighed in on secrecy. Papers took sides by the day. Kept as a bundle, the week shows the tempo of the fight in mid-March 1980: a bill, a statement, a headline, and an agency reading its own future in the press.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501380001-7:
Press clippings for May 1980 carry a file head on the Iran mission. It goes on and on, the head says of the story. A New York Times piece by Seymour M Hersh, dated 1 May 1980, leads the sampled pages. It treats the failed bid to free the hostages in Tehran. The appeal of a Hollywood thriller opens his account.

Commandos swept toward the embassy in the plan he retells. The mission ended in desert wreckage instead. The month's pages judge what went wrong and who should answer. The file is the press record of a national wound, kept by the agency whose world the mission had crossed that spring.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601730001-7:
Staffing forecasts for operations professionals are forwarded in a short memo from Harry E. Fitzwater. Fitzwater, Director of Personnel, sent the papers for information and possible follow-up talk. At the core is a mid-June model of how many staff leave over time.

The model shows that loss rates shift as the age mix changes over five years. For that reason no single yearly intake holds strength steady, the papers argue. Career staff comments sort new staff into operations officers, direct-hire specialists, and internal moves. Intake ranges for fiscal 1980 to 1983 are given, though many figures are redacted in the released text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601820001-7:
Background papers on the President's power to reshape the executive branch fill a White House pack dated April 1977. A 7 April 1977 memo from Jack Watson sends the pack to cabinet members. It was set as reading for Bert Lance's talk at the 11 April cabinet meeting.

Contents run from a signing statement to the full Reorganization Act of 1977. The President signed the act on 6 April 1977, the press note states. Question and answer pages explain how plans go to Congress and take effect. Background pages trace past reshaping efforts and list sources for further reading on the topic.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100040001-7:
A revised set of economic tables is issued in a handbook dated 15 October 1957. The volume is research aid CIA/RR RA-12-R1 from the Office of Research and Reports. Front notes explain marks, rounding to three key digits, and the term negligible.

Tables set NATO and bloc output side by side across many goods. One table tracks meat output in 1938, 1946, 1948, and 1950 to 1956, plus 1960 plan aims. A fish table gives landed weights by country for the same span. Totals are built from unrounded data, so printed parts may not sum exactly, the notes warn.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100130001-7:
Economic profiles and tables fill the 1966 handbook, marked H 66-1 and dated July 1966. The Directorate of Intelligence issued the volume for staff reference. Opening profile pages give land mass, people, and gross product for blocs and states in 1965 terms.

United States gross product is put at 664.1 billion dollars for 1965 on those pages. Canada is put at 50 billion and Cuba at 3.05 billion in 1957 prices. Later tables count Communist economic and arms experts posted in poorer free states through 1965. Counts are split by the USSR, East Europe, and China for each host land.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000200210001-7:
Copy number 1 of the 1974 handbook was prepared by the Office of Economic Research. The volume gives figures for chosen non-Communist lands and all Communist lands. Most data cover the years 1965 to 1973, the preface states. Queries and comments on the volume are welcomed on the title page.

Summary tables cover the United States, Japan, the European Community, the USSR, East Europe, and China. Footnotes give terms, odd cases, and methods in full, with fuller terms on the goods tables than on the summary pages. One table tracks installed electric power capacity in million kilowatts from 1965 on. United States capacity in that table climbs from about 255 to about 438 by 1973. Japan in the same table climbs from 41 to about 85 across the years shown.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-02247r000200200001-7:
Short place notes on the Vakhsh River valley and Fergana fill a card file drawn from Soviet sources. One note, sourced to Trud number 36, treats Kurgan-Tyube in the Tadzhik SSR. The valley is called the cotton centre of the land for fine fibre cotton.

The town is listed with a hospital, a library, a teaching school, and a House of Culture. A ruined citadel on a hill marks the town entry, the note states. A second note treats the Fergana Canal and its oasis by the upper Syr-Darya. It recalls that in 1917 much of the valley had no watering works at all.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-00750r000101470001-7:
Family members who work abroad gain a path to career posts in an executive order dated 15 May 1982. The order is titled Overseas Employment and was issued for instant release. It rests on sections 3301 and 3302 of Title 5 and section 301 of Title 3.

A citizen family member with 24 months of good service abroad may be hired at home without contest. Posts at home lie in the executive branch, Guam, Puerto Rico, and the Virgin Islands included. Terms require local hire abroad, a good rating, and service after 1 January 1980. Further terms set a ten year span in which the months must fall.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10m00666r000503450008-7:
Secret Service material not yet sent to the President's Commission is listed in Commission No. 67. Richard Helms, Deputy Director for Plans, wrote to Mr. J. Lee Rankin. The memo answers a 12 February request from the Commission side.
